message.content:
To evaluate the definite integral  

\[
\int_{1}^{3} x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x ,
\]

first find an antiderivative \(F(x)\):

\[
F(x)= \frac{x^{3}}{3}.
\]

Now apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{1}^{3} x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x 
&= F(3)-F(1)\\[4pt]
&=\left(\frac{3^{3}}{3}\right)-\left(\frac{1^{3}}{3}\right) \\[4pt]
&=\frac{27}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\\[4pt]
&=\frac{26}{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]

So,

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \int_{1}^{3} x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{26}{3}}
\]
message.reasoning:
The user asks "Find the definite integral of f(x) = x^2 from x=1 to x=3." That's straightforward calculus: ∫_1^3 x^2 dx = [x^3/3]_1^3 = (27/3 - 1/3) = (9 - 0.333...) = 8.666... or exactly 26/3? Wait compute precisely: 27/3 = 9; 1/3 ≈ .333..., difference = 8 + 2/3 = 26/3.

Thus answer: 26/3.
